thread.title: The MnM Portfolio - Reviewing May 2018 Fundamentals

author: MnMInvestor
title: The MnM Portfolio - Reviewing May 2018 Fundamentals
text:
My Fundamental Review Process It’s been about three months since I last reported on the fundamentals of the stocks in my MnM Portfolio. Periodically, I review my portfolio’s holdings to take stock of how my holdings are doing and to assist with the allocation of incoming dividends.
As I have noted in the past, I rely heavily upon the data compiled by SeekingAlpha as well as FASTgraphs.com and then crunch the numbers a little on my own. I have long held the belief that FASTgraphs is an excellent service and has served me well in my dividend growth pursuits. I do not have any relationship with the service, I am just a user and believer in their product.
As I present my current analysis let me quickly state that my approach to fundamentals has not changed. I have a long-term investment outlook, as my anticipated retirement is still several decades away. I look not only to P/E multiples and dividend yields, but also put a degree of emphasis on investing in companies that are effectively growing their earnings. The emphasis on ‘growth’ was a prominent theme this quarter when I rebalanced the MnM Portfolio by selling a number of slow/no-growers. I replaced them with superior dividend and earnings growers.
In the following section I will present the portfolio stocks including relevant price, dividend yield and P/E ratios. In addition I have created a basic PEG ratio to complement the standard P/E ratio, which incorporates growth rates. When I am considering where to reinvest my dividends, I am looking to buy shares of dividend growth stocks that are trading off of their historical P/E ratios and also have relatively low PEG Ratios (sub-2 is where I like to operate).
Once I have the fundamental picture, I work to understand why the stocks are trading where they are. Overall I am bullish on all of the stocks within the portfolio, otherwise why hold them; however this screen helps identify when it’s best to invest in particular stocks/sectors. As we all know the market sees stocks, and even sectors, quickly go in and out of fashion. Buying at the right time and at the right price can lead to improved long-term results.
May 2018 Fundamental Review Going forward I intend to present my analysis quarterly, and similar to what was presented in February, I obtained stock price as well as P/E ratios and growth rates from FASTgraphs.com . Using these figures I first compared the current P/E to the historical P/E (think of this as an average P/E) over a five-year timeframe to assess where the stocks are trading relative to their average multiple. I then pulled the growth rates from FASTgraphs.com for the same timeframe and divided the current P/E by it to determine a PEG ratio. I also want to have the ability to see how much I am paying for the stocks’ ability to grow their earnings.
When I reviewed the data I highlighted those stocks in red which tended to have both excessive P/E ratios as well as high PEG ratios. These tend to be overbought and in some cases also have very little earnings growth. Items highlighted in green tended to be trading below historical P/E ratios yet generally had high levels of growth.
Note: Prices are obviously not current, but were reported within the past couple of days and serve as reference points.
Fundamental Review Findings – P/E Changes Since Q1 First, we’ve seen some interesting developments in prices since I last wrote in February. When I compare basic P/E ratios of the stocks in the portfolio to my last article, we see that REITs have gotten more expensive while the bulk of the common equities have gotten cheaper.
I’m not sure if we are going to call it a bottom, but the REITs seem to have found some momentum this quarter. We'll see if it holds.
Within the portfolio there were only three common equities that appreciated. Apple ( AAPL ) saw pricing momentum following a stronger than expected quarter and continued investment in the company by Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.B ). Hormel ( HRL ) was essentially flat, trading only slightly higher, while Sysco ( SYY ) too saw bullish pricing momentum on an earnings beat this quarter.
Note: I didn’t compare the new names to the portfolio, which include: Corning ( GLW ), Intel ( INTC ), Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ), Pepsico ( PEP ) or Prudential ( PRU ), as I do not have reference data from last quarter. I will compare these in the next quarterly update. Those who follow my articles regularly will soon see that Pepsi was introduced to the portfolio just this month.
Fundamental Review Findings – Not a Ton of Changes Overall, despite the downward movement in many of the common equities, the most fundamentally attractive names remain First Horizon (NYSE: FHN ), Starbucks (NASDAQ: SBUX ) and J M Smucker (NYSE: SJM ). First Horizon and Smucker both have relatively low P/E’s combined with double-digit earnings growth. Starbucks is a little bit more of a battleground stock, as its recent growth has not been at the level it was in the past and it seems most are betting on growth in China. It still commands a relatively high P/E ratio as well.
In addition to those three I am seeing positive fundamentals with a number of other stocks including: Amgen ( AMGN ), 3M ( MMM ), Johnson & Johnson, Illinois Tool Works ( ITW ), Corning, US Bank ( USB ) and AT&T ( T ). As noted above, the sell-off in the industrials sector has brought some much overdue opportunity with regard to 3M and Illinois Tool Works. It may be time to add to these.
Looking more closely at Johnson & Johnson I almost can’t believe I’m seeing it with a near 3% yield. It felt like the stock would never yield above 2.5% these last couple of years. It's finally much closer to fair value than it has been in some time.
I was hesitant to call out AT&T as a screaming buy on the fundamentals given that it is somewhat of a battleground stock. It will be another month or so before we hear the judge’s decision on the anti-trust suit brought by the government against its merger with Time Warner ( TWX ). I’m optimistic that the merger will go through, and it’s hard to argue with a 6+% yield, though it should be noted that the company is heavily levered and does not have robust growth. It's cheap, but there's a lot going on there and it's not growing like many other names in the portfolio are.
Takeaways I have mentioned this in the past, but as always, it’s important to note that the fundamentals on their own do not give the entire picture of a stock. For example, when I look over the stocks that I sold back in April, it would seem like CVS Health ( CVS ) and Cardinal Health ( CAH ) are now screaming buys. Even General Mills ( GIS ) and Patterson Dental ( PDCO ) are trading significantly off their average multiples.
While these names are fundamentally cheap, they ultimately didn’t fit my model of dividend growth anymore as they are either exhibiting no dividend growth (as in CVS, General Mills, Patterson Dental) or limited growth (Cardinal Health). I get that they are using a lot of cash to grow their business, but I'm not going to hang around to find out when I can shift the money to others whom are doing much better.
My exercise of selling dividend growth laggards and replacing them with stronger growers, which I wrote about here , was effective. The average of all the growth rates in my current portfolio as it stands today increased to (7.7%) as compared to the rate from February (6.8%). This should translate into higher dividends in the future.
Overall I am encouraged to see that there are some great stocks trading at fair prices. The banks, industrials, telecoms and consumer staples stocks all seem to be fundamentally sitting in the buy zone right now. I will leave it to you to decide what is right for you to be buying right now, but hopefully this analysis was useful to you in your pursuit of dividend growth investing.
Disclosure: I am/we are long THE STOCKS LISTED IN THE PORTFOLIO.
